question: Which of the five has been most explicit about serving mass-affluent clients, and what exactly have they said?

claims.text: On how explicitly each firm names the mass-affluent client segment, the comparison can only be made partially: Merrill explicitly names a 'Mass Affluent' segment and is the only one of the five to do so, while Morgan Stanley, Schwab, Edward Jones and Raymond James do not use the term 'mass-affluent' at all in the passages searched and instead name other (wealthier or broader) segments, and industry-research sources contain no statement. Because the firms describe different segments (Merrill's Mass Affluent of $500K–$1MM versus the others' high-net-worth/ultra-high-net-worth/affluent/individual-investor labels), the five are not directly comparable on a single definition of mass-affluent.

Merrill: Merrill's investor-day presentation defines the Wealth Continuum of client segments, listing 'Mass Affluent ($500K - $1MM)' and 'High Net Worth ($1MM - $10MM)'. Why it might matter: per the same presentation, this Wealth Continuum is Merrill's 'engine for lasting growth,' so naming the mass-affluent tier within it frames how the firm organizes its client coverage.

Schwab: Schwab's 10-K states that Schwab Private Client Services serves clients with $1 million to $10 million in qualifying assets and Schwab Private Wealth Services serves clients with more than $10 million, offering dedicated service teams and specialized expertise.
Schwab: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said about one-third of new clients are affluent, alongside a growing volume of new trader clients.
Schwab: Schwab's investor deck states 68% of affluent investors want and are willing to pay for advice.
Merrill: Merrill's investor-day presentation defines the Wealth Continuum of client segments, listing 'Mass Affluent ($500K - $1MM)' and 'High Net Worth ($1MM - $10MM)'.
Merrill: Merrill Wealth Management's advisory business is described as focusing on clients with over $250,000 in total investable assets.
Schwab: Schwab's materials describe a segment as 'retail investor households with >$500K in investable assets with Schwab.'

Schwab: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster stated that 61% of affluent clients ages 25 to 44 prefer to consolidate their wealth and banking relationships, which he cited amid a 'bull market for convenience' driving investors to consolidate their financial lives.
Schwab: Wurster added that households with $1 million to $5 million in assets using only one financial services firm rose to 22%, up 11 percentage points year-over-year, which he expects to grow.
Schwab: Schwab Advisor Services head Jon Beatty said there is 'a bull market for advice,' noting that 68% of affluent Americans say they are willing to pay for advice today, up from 38% in 2010.
Schwab: Schwab's investor day deck states that 68% of affluent investors want and are willing to pay for advice.
Schwab: Schwab's Q2 2026 deck notes that 61% of affluent clients prefer to consolidate wealth and banking relationships.
Merrill: Merrill's investor-day deck presents a 'Wealth Continuum' that defines the 'Mass Affluent' segment as clients with $500K to $1MM, above which sits 'High Net Worth' ($1MM - $10MM).
Merrill: Merrill's most recent statement (3Q26, published 2026-10-14) reports that Merrill added about 4,200 net new households with at least $500,000 in assets, up 17%.
Merrill: In 3Q26 Merrill added ~4.2K net new $500K+ households, per the Merrill Wealth Management Highlights.
Merrill: In 3Q26 Merrill and the Private Bank together added ~5K net new $500K+ relationships.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley describes the clients of its Wealth Management segment as individual investors, including high and ultra-high net worth individuals, and businesses and institutions; it does not name a 'mass-affluent' client segment.
adjacent.differs_because: Morgan Stanley names 'high and ultra-high net worth individuals' (a higher wealth tier) as its wealth client segment, and uses 'ultra-high net worth' for its lending/institutional clients; it does not name a 'mass-affluent' segment. The only 'mass-affluent' mention is a third-party Cerulli Associates figure about 401(k) participants, not Morgan Stanley's own segment.

adjacent.text: Schwab: Schwab states that 61% of affluent clients ages 25 to 44 prefer to consolidate their wealth and banking relationships.
adjacent.differs_because: Schwab uses the terms 'affluent' and wealth-tier labels ('high net worth', 'ultra-high net worth', households with $1 million to $5 million) but does not use the specific 'mass-affluent' segment name.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Raymond James's Wealth Strategies offering is described as bringing 'the best of our firm to your high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients,' naming the high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth segments rather than mass-affluent.
adjacent.differs_because: RJF names the 'high-net-worth' and 'ultra-high-net-worth' client segments (its Private Wealth Advisor program defines high-net-worth as at least $5 million in investable assets), not the 'mass-affluent' segment. No passage names the mass-affluent segment.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley: A Morgan Stanley executive described a 'more democratized offering' of alternatives to go to the firm's retail client base, referencing retail clients rather than mass-affluent clients.
adjacent.differs_because: The firm describes serving 'individual investors' (specifically 'high and ultra-high net worth individuals') and 'retail' clients, but does not use the term 'mass-affluent'; these are different (wealthier or broader) client segments.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: Edward Jones lists 'High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients' among its new client-targeting initiatives.
adjacent.differs_because: No passage uses the term 'mass-affluent'; Edward Jones describes serving 'individual investors' and 'long-term investors' (broader client categories) and explicitly targets 'high net worth' clients (a wealthier segment), rather than naming mass-affluent clients.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Tash Elwyn, president of Raymond James' Private Client Group, said the firm is committed to being a destination for private wealth advisors and their clients, stating that individuals and families with significant wealth require truly personal advice backed by the right resources.
adjacent.differs_because: The firm's statements concern high-net-worth, ultra-high-net-worth and private wealth clients (wealthier segments, generally defined as $5M+ in investable assets), not mass-affluent clients; no passage contains any statement about mass-affluent clients specifically.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley: Ted Pick describes serving clients across all three wealth channels, including the 'everyday transaction offering' and CashPlus in E*TRADE, and the Workplace channel to partner with companies to reach employees.
adjacent.differs_because: Morgan Stanley describes targeting and serving a broad base of retail/individual/'everyday' clients (via E*TRADE and Workplace channels) rather than using 'mass-affluent' terminology or naming a mass-affluent segment specifically; these are wider segments that contain mass-affluent clients.

adjacent.text: Schwab: Schwab states that about one-third of its new clients are affluent, and that it is winning with investors of all ages, wealth tiers, and time horizons.
adjacent.differs_because: Schwab describes targeting 'affluent' and 'higher net worth' clients (including households with $1 million to $5 million in assets), which are wealth tiers above the mass-affluent segment; the passages never use the specific term 'mass-affluent'.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: Edward Jones states that its initiatives include targeting new clients, specifically a 'High Net Worth' initiative focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients.
adjacent.differs_because: The passage describes targeting High Net Worth clients (a higher wealth tier) rather than mass-affluent clients; mass-affluent is not mentioned anywhere.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry states that the firm's private wealth advisor program and expanded alternative investments platform support advisors who focus on high-net-worth clients.
adjacent.differs_because: Passages describe targeting high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients (e.g., at least $5 million or $50 million in investable assets), a wealthier segment than mass-affluent clients; no passage mentions mass-affluent clients.

adjacent.text: Schwab: Schwab states that for clients with more substantial needs, Schwab Private Client Services (for clients with $1 million to $10 million in qualifying assets) and Schwab Private Wealth Services (for clients with more than $10 million) provide enhanced, relationship-based experiences including dedicated service teams, specialized expertise, expedited processing, pricing advantages, and access to exclusive product offerings.
adjacent.differs_because: These offerings are described for 'affluent' clients and high-net-worth tiers ($1 million to $10 million and above $10 million in qualifying assets), which is a different (higher/broader) segment than 'mass-affluent' (typically roughly $100,000 to $1 million); no passage uses the term 'mass-affluent' or describes a mass-affluent-specific product, service, platform, or fee level.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: The Partnership states it offers clients a variety of solutions including investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings.
adjacent.differs_because: No passage mentions 'mass-affluent' clients; the products, services, and fee structures described are offered to the firm's clients/individual investors generally, which is a broader group than the mass-affluent segment asked about.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Raymond James states that through its PCG segment it provides financial planning, investment advisory, and securities transaction services for which it generally charges either asset-based fees or sales commissions.
adjacent.differs_because: The passages describe products, services, platforms, and fee structures offered to the firm's clients generally (e.g., Private Client Group clients), a wider group than mass-affluent clients specifically; no passage mentions 'mass-affluent' clients.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Raymond James' Private Wealth Advisor designation program is for advisors who specialize in high-net-worth clients, which the firm generally defines as those with at least $5 million in investable assets.
adjacent.differs_because: Defines the high-net-worth client segment (at least $5 million in investable assets), not the mass-affluent segment the sub-question asks about.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley said its strategy is to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice, which it says sets its franchise apart and positions it to continue to outperform.
adjacent.differs_because: The passage refers to 'retail clients' broadly, not specifically 'mass-affluent' clients; retail is a broader category that includes mass-affluent and other client tiers.

gaps.what: Morgan Stanley - names the mass-affluent client segment: Morgan Stanley names 'high and ultra-high net worth individuals' as its wealth segment and does not name a mass-affluent segment; the only 'mass-affluent' mention is a third-party Cerulli Associates figure about 401(k) participants.
gaps.suggested_source: Morgan Stanley investor materials that explicitly name a mass-affluent client segment, if any

gaps.what: Edward Jones - whether and how explicitly it names the mass-affluent client segment: no passage names the mass-affluent segment.
gaps.suggested_source: Edward Jones disclosures explicitly naming a mass-affluent segment

gaps.what: Schwab - names the mass-affluent client segment: Schwab uses 'affluent' and wealth-tier labels but not the specific 'mass-affluent' segment name.
Raymond James - names the mass-affluent client segment: RJF names high-net-worth/ultra-high-net-worth segments, not mass-affluent.
Industry research - names the mass-affluent client segment: no item in the sources describes an industry-level naming of the mass-affluent segment.
gaps.suggested_source: Industry research explicitly characterizing the mass-affluent segment
